# Dedup, record and assembly — Turn 4 and Turn 5

This file holds the two turns that run **after the 12 agents return**: Turn 4
deduplicates, gates, tags and records each pass, and Turn 5 assembles and prints
the one report. `SKILL.md` keeps the name of each turn and the condition that
decides whether it runs; the procedure is here.

The orchestrator reads this file **once, in Turn 3b**, while it waits for the
agents. It stays in context for the later passes of a loop.

Both turns use `{stamp}`, `{bundle_dir}`, `{passes}`, `{resolved_path}` and
`{project-name}` exactly as `SKILL.md` set them.

---

## Turn 4

**Turn 4 — Deduplicate, validate & record.** Runs **every pass**, and it is the end of the loop body: deduplicate this pass's agent results, gate-evaluate, tag, record the pass, write the ledger. **It prints no report** — there is exactly one report per scan and Turn 5 prints it. Do NOT print an intermediate dedup list.

> **This turn used to print the report and clean up, and both moved.** The report moved to Turn 5 so that a 1-pass scan and an N-pass scan take the **same** path through this turn — the "1 pass is byte-identical to today" constraint is easier to hold with one report writer than with a last pass that doubles as one. The auto-clean moved to Turn 5 because, left here, pass 1 deletes what pass 2 needs: `source.md`, the ledger photocopy and the accumulating rows file. A later editor must not move either back.

Then, after the loop body has run `{passes}` times (or stopped early), go to Turn 5 once.

1. **Dedup.** Parse every FINDING and LEAD from the 12 agents. Group by `group_key` (Contract | function | bug-class). Exact-match first; merge synonymous bug_class within same (Contract, function). Keep best per group, number sequentially, annotate `[agents: N]`.

   **MANDATORY — Canonicalise the bug-class label (HARD GATE).** Before grouping, for every (Contract, function) whose agents used **more than one** bug-class label, choose **one** label and rewrite every one of those findings to carry it. Then group.

   Choose in this order, and stop at the first that applies:
   1. A label already listed for that same contract and function in `{bundle_dir}/known-findings.md` — the repository's own word wins, always.
   2. Otherwise the label that most agents used.
   3. Otherwise the shortest label that names the **defect**, not its consequence. `zero-abort-address` over `abort-address-zero-burns-funds`.

   Merging under one label is only correct when the labels name the **same class of bug**. Two genuinely different bugs in one function keep two labels and stay two records — function isolation is about functions, and this rule is about words.

   **Why this is a gate and not a nicety.** The per-function vocabulary that keeps a key stable only constrains what an **earlier scan** wrote. A class discovered mid-scan is constrained by nothing, and a real scan proved what follows: three agents in one pass named one bug `zero-abort-address`, `unregistered-abort-address` and `abort-address-zero-burns-funds`, and the over-approval class drew three labels across three passes. Unfixed, that is three ledger records for one bug, three lines in every future `known-findings.md`, and one bug that is never recognised again. This step is the only thing standing between the fork and the ledger. Canonicalise here and the next pass inherits the canonical label, so the fork closes after one scan.

   **MANDATORY — Wide-description (group_key).** Merged group with distinct mechanisms (different `fix:`, code-level cause, or attack path) MUST list every mechanism. No dropping. Same function can have multiple coexisting bugs at the same group_key — all MUST appear.

   **MANDATORY — Function-level second pass (after group_key dedup).** Run at (Contract, function), ignoring bug_class. Agents often label coexisting bugs with different bug_class tags but reference multiple mechanisms in the body. For every (Contract, function) with multiple final findings: scan body (description, path, proof, fix) of every constituent for distinct mechanisms across bug_class boundaries. Every mechanism in any constituent body MUST appear in ≥1 final finding.

   **MANDATORY — Function isolation (HARD).** NEVER merge across different `function:` fields. Dedup only within (Contract, function). Different function = different bug. Second pass above stays WITHIN (Contract, function), never across.

   **MANDATORY — Fix preservation (HARD GATE).** Before writing merged `fix:` on a multi-finding (Contract, function):
   1. Collect every raw `fix:` from agents flagging the tuple.
   2. Group by ADD-lines (`+` lines, or equivalent require/assignment).
   3. Distinct if ADD-lines differ in: called function/expression (e.g., `require(msg.value == amount)` vs `require(zrc20 != _ETH_ADDRESS_)`), check direction (validate/restrict/ban), or checked parameter.
   4. ≥2 distinct → present as Option A, B, … — one block per distinct fix, verbatim from agent text (no paraphrase).
   5. Label intuitively: validate / restrict / allow-and-handle / ban-path.

   **Output format when 2+ distinct fixes exist:**

   ```
   **Fix (Option A — <label>)**:

   ```diff
   <verbatim diff from raw agent N1's fix>
   ```

   **Fix (Option B — <label>)**:

   ```diff
   <verbatim diff from raw agent N2's fix>
   ```
   ```

   **Inline check before printing**: count distinct fixes from raw for this (Contract, function). ≥2 distinct but merged shows 1 → violation, add alternatives.

   **MANDATORY — Completeness (HARD GATE).** Before print: list every unique (Contract, function, bug-class) in any raw FINDING/LEAD across the 12 agents. Every unique (Contract, function) MUST have ≥1 item in final. Zero = silent drop, fix it. Multiple bug-class within same (Contract, function) MAY collapse to one item (wide-description), but the (Contract, function) MUST survive. Print inline before report: `Completeness: N unique (Contract, function) in raw, N covered in final.`

   Composite chains: if A's output feeds B's precondition AND combined impact > either alone, add `Chain: [A] + [B]` at conf = min(A, B). Most audits: 0–2.

2. **Gate.** Run each deduped finding through the four gates in `judging.md` (no skip, no reorder, no revisit after verdict).

   **Single-pass:** every relevant code path ONCE in fixed order (constructor → setters → swap → mint → burn → liquidate). One-line verdict: `BLOCKS` / `ALLOWS` / `IRRELEVANT` / `UNCERTAIN`. `UNCERTAIN = ALLOWS`. Commit, no re-examination.

3. **Lead promotion / rejection.**
   - LEAD → FINDING (conf 75) if: full exploit chain in source, OR `[agents: 2+]` demoted (not rejected) same issue.
   - `[agents: 2+]` does NOT override a code path that interrupts attack before harm — demote to LEAD if execution uncertain.
   - No deployer-intent reasoning — what code allows, not how deployer might use it.

4. **Memory tag.** **SKIP this step entirely when memory is off.** It comes before the report, not after it, because the report prints what it decides. It is a **lookup, never a judgment** — no finding is re-argued here, and no verdict from the gate is revisited.

   a. **Build the key** for every gated FINDING and every gated LEAD — the three segments of Turn 4's `group_key`, each normalised **on its own** (lower case, every run of non-alphanumeric characters to one hyphen), then joined with `|`: `vault|withdraw|reentrancy`. Normalise the segments separately, never the joined string, or the separators become hyphens too.

   **The bug-class segment is where memory succeeds or fails.** Before writing a key, read the per-function vocabulary back from `{bundle_dir}/known-findings.md` — the same file the agents were given: *if this finding is one of the bug classes already listed for this same contract and function, write that exact label. Invent a new label only when none of them is the same class of bug.* This is the only judgment in the whole memory path, and it happens when the label is **written** — never at merge time. The keys built here are the keys step 6 writes; build them once.

   b. **Tag each finding and each lead.** Look its key up in the pre-scan key list:

   ```bash
   tail -n +2 {bundle_dir}/memory-before.tsv | cut -f1,3 | sort > {bundle_dir}/known-keys.tsv
   ```

   Key present → **KNOWN**, printed as `KNOWN (n scans)` where **n is column 2 plus one**. The scan that is printing has found it again, so the count the report shows is the count the ledger will hold when step 6 has written it — report and file say the same number. Key absent → **NEW**. Nothing else decides this tag.

   The lookup is against the **pre-scan photocopy**, in every pass of a loop. `KNOWN` means "an earlier **scan** recorded this"; a finding first raised by pass 1 of this scan is still `NEW` in pass 3, and how many passes saw it is what `seen in k/N runs` says. Tagging against the live ledger would make pass 2 call this scan's own work old news.

   c. **Write this run's keys** to `{bundle_dir}/run-keys.tsv`, one per line, from step 4a.

   The "Known from earlier scans" rows are **not** built here. They are report work, and a pass that built them could not know what a later pass is about to raise. They are built once, in Turn 5.

5. **Record the pass.** Do NOT print the report.

   a. **Write the run file** to `.solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/run-K.md`, where `K` is the pass number. **Every pass of every scan writes one**, at any pass count, `{passes}` of 1 included. This is the only place this pass's work is recorded, and Turn 5 assembles the report out of these files — a pass that writes no run file has produced nothing the report can print.

   One directory per scan, one file per run; `ls` is history in order. The git SHA goes **inside** the file, not in the directory name, so two scans of the same commit sit side by side instead of colliding. Nothing deletes these files, and `--file-output` does not govern them — they are memory, not reports.

   **The file, exactly:**

   ````markdown
   # Run K — solidity-auditor

   <!--RUN pass=K of=N stamp={stamp} sha=abc1234 agents=11/12-->

   Pass K of N · <date> · `abc1234` · 11/12 agents returned — the access-control agent died.

   ## Findings

   <finding blocks, kind=FINDING>

   ## Leads

   <finding blocks, kind=LEAD>
   ````

   The sentence is for the human; the `<!--RUN-->` marker is what shell reads. `agents=11/12` is where the `Passes` row gets its degradation text, so a lost agent is on disk and not only in a printed line that scrolls away — and the dead agent's **name** stays here, in the sentence, and never enters the Scope table.

   **These two headings and no others, in every run.** No `## New findings` in a later run — newness is already carried by the `NEW` / `KNOWN` tag and by `seen in k/N runs`, and a heading saying it again is a second source of truth that can disagree with the first. **No "verified clean", "checked" or "sound" section, under any name.** A path a pass did not raise is not a path a pass cleared, and a real scan invented such a section unasked. Nothing ever reads it back, and it is the same overstated-coverage defect this whole design exists to kill.

   **The finding block, exactly:**

   ````markdown
   <!--F key=contract|function|bug-class conf=95 kind=FINDING agents=8-->

   [95] **<Title>**

   `ContractName.functionName` · Confidence: 95

   **Description**
   <the vulnerable pattern and why it is exploitable, 1 short sentence>

   **Fix**

   ```diff
   - vulnerable line(s)
   + fixed line(s)
   ```

   <!--/F-->
   ````

   - **The markers bound the block.** `<!--F ` opens it, `<!--/F-->` closes it, each on its own line at the start of the line. **Never `---`**: today's separator also appears inside a unified diff (`--- a/Vault.sol`), so it cannot cut a block that now carries one. The HTML comment renders invisible, so the file still reads as human memory.
   - **`key`** — exactly the key step 4a built, unchanged. Never re-derived here. The same key the ledger stores, so the run file and `memory.tsv` agree by construction.
   - **`conf`** — an integer, on `kind=FINDING` blocks only. **A `kind=LEAD` block carries no `conf` attribute at all** — a lead is not scored, and writing `0` would sort it against real numbers.
   - **`kind`** — `FINDING` or `LEAD`.
   - **`agents`** — carried from `[agents: 8]`. Informational; nothing parses it.

   **Write the markers exactly as printed.** They are the only thing standing between a finding and a silent loss: the assembler counts open markers against close markers against readable blocks, and a disagreement becomes a visible `**Run files**` row in the report saying how many findings could not be read. The report may print **less** than the scan found; it may never claim to print **more**. A fudged marker costs a visible warning, not a hidden hole — but it still costs the finding.

   **Above and below the threshold, the block shape is identical.** A block whose `conf` is below 75 simply has no `**Fix**` section. The run file does **not** mark which side of the line a finding sits on; the assembler re-derives that from `conf`. One source of truth.

   **Write the Description and the diff Fix block here, in full.** This is the expensive per-finding writing, and it is paid **now**, in the pass that found the bug, while that pass still has context to spare. Turn 5 re-words nothing — it pastes these bytes into the report. An orchestrator drafting seventy findings at the end of a long scan is the failure this ordering exists to prevent.

   **The title and the Description are written in Simplified Technical English**, per `{resolved_path}/report-language.md`, which Turn 2 read. Because Turn 5 re-words nothing, this is the **only** step where the report's sentences can be made readable — there is no later cleanup pass and there must never be one. Four pieces of text obey that file: the title, the Description, the Lead description, and the Lead's code-smell list.

   Three things it does **not** reach, and a later editor must not extend it to them: the **diff** inside the Fix block, which is pasted verbatim from the agent, the **bug-class label** in the `key` attribute, which is a memory key and is chosen by step 1 and step 4a, and the **identifiers** on the location line, which are spelled as the source spells them. Softening a label to read better writes a second ledger record for one bug.

   Where the agent handed up a sentence that already meets the rules, keep the agent's words. Where it did not — a metaphor, an `-ing` clause, forty words, `catastrophic` — rewrite the sentence and keep the claim. Rewriting is about the wording only: the mechanism, the actor and the effect the agent proved are not up for revision here, and the gate has already run.

   **Then record the agent count**, once per pass, always, `12/12` included:

   ```bash
   printf '%s\t%s\n' pass_{K}_agents "11/12" >> .solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/scope.tsv
   ```

   Written only when a pass ran short, a missing key would mean two different things — a whole pass and a lost pass — and the assembler could not tell them apart.

   b. **Print one summary line**, only when `{passes}` is above 1, and nothing else — the last thing the pass does, after step 6 has written the ledger. It is the only thing the runner sees for minutes at a time, so it answers two questions: how far along, and is the loop still learning?

   ```
   Pass 2/3 — 17 findings (3 new) · 6 leads (2 new) · ledger 41 records
   ```

   - The counts are post-dedup and post-gate — the numbers `run-2.md` holds, not raw agent output.
   - **new** = the key was not in the ledger before this pass. A lookup, not a judgment.
   - `ledger N records` is the row count of `.solidity-auditor/memory.tsv` after step 6 has written it, so print this line after step 6.
   - The parentheses are printed **only when the ledger was non-empty when the scan started**. On a first-ever scan every key is new and they say nothing: `Pass 1/3 — 17 findings · 6 leads · ledger 17 records`.
   - When a pass lost an agent, the line gains a clause: `Pass 2/3 — 15 findings (2 new) · 6 leads (0 new) · ledger 39 records · 11/12 agents`.
   - When **both** new-counts are zero, the line ends with `· no new ground`. That is the loop's most informative outcome — the passes have converged — and it must not have to be inferred from two zeros:

   ```
   Pass 3/3 — 17 findings (0 new) · 6 leads (0 new) · ledger 41 records · no new ground
   ```

   Elapsed time is deliberately not printed: it needs a `date` call either side of every pass, and the runner's terminal already shows wall-clock.

   > **On a 1-pass scan this whole step prints nothing.** Step 5a still writes `run-1.md` — silently. `Pass 1/1 — …` is a progress line for a loop that is not running, and the plain path prints the bytes it printed before loop mode existed. Writing a file is not printing; the freeze covers printed output.

6. **Memory write.** **SKIP this step entirely when memory is off.** It is a step of Turn 4 and not a turn of its own because it can only be built from this turn's gated findings — the rows do not exist until the gate has run.

   a. **Build this run's rows** from the keys step 4 already built. One row per gated FINDING and per gated LEAD, four tab-separated columns:

   ```
   key	sha	title	kind
   ```

   - `key` — exactly the key step 4a built and step 4b tagged. Never rebuilt here: a key that differs between the tag and the row would report `NEW` and store a duplicate.
   - `sha` — `git rev-parse --short HEAD`. Not a git repo, or a repo with no commits: write `none` and carry on. The SHA is never part of the match, so a missing one costs nothing.
   - `title` — the finding title, tabs and newlines replaced by a single space, cut to 80 characters. Bars are safe: only the key is ever split on bars.
   - `kind` — `FINDING` or `LEAD`.

   Append the rows to the accumulating file, do not overwrite it:

   ```bash
   cat >> {bundle_dir}/scan-rows.tsv
   ```

   b. **Merge.** One `awk` pass over the photocopy and this scan's accumulated rows. `sort` + `join` is not used: `join` returns only matching rows, so keeping old-only and new-only rows would need three invocations and identical sort order across locales.

   ```bash
   awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
   FILENAME==ARGV[1] {
     if (FNR==1) next
     o_st[$1]=$2; o_sc[$1]=$3; o_sha[$1]=$4; o_ti[$1]=$5; o_ki[$1]=$6
     if (!($1 in o_seen)) { o_seen[$1]=1; oord[++on]=$1 }
     next
   }
   {
     if (!($1 in n_seen)) { n_seen[$1]=1; nord[++nn]=$1 }
     n_sha[$1]=$2; n_ti[$1]=$3; n_ki[$1]=$4
   }
   END {
     print "#solidity-auditor-memory v1", "key", "status", "scans", "sha", "title", "kind"
     for (i=1; i<=on; i++) {
       k = oord[i]
       if (k in n_seen) print k, "KNOWN", o_sc[k]+1, n_sha[k], n_ti[k], n_ki[k]
       else             print k, o_st[k], o_sc[k], o_sha[k], o_ti[k], o_ki[k]
     }
     for (i=1; i<=nn; i++) {
       k = nord[i]
       if (!(k in o_seen)) print k, "NEW", 1, n_sha[k], n_ti[k], n_ki[k]
     }
   }
   ' {bundle_dir}/memory-before.tsv {bundle_dir}/scan-rows.tsv > .solidity-auditor/memory.tsv.tmp
   ```

   The three cases, all visible in one command:

   | Case | Result |
   |---|---|
   | Old row re-found | `status` `KNOWN`, `scans` + 1, `sha` / `title` / `kind` taken from **this scan's** row |
   | Old row not re-found | carried over completely unchanged |
   | No old row | `status` `NEW`, `scans` 1 |

   Two rules the merge carries, and a later editor must not simplify away:

   - **`kind` is not part of the key.** A Lead an earlier scan recorded and this scan proved is the *same bug*: its `kind` flips to `FINDING` in place, `scans` keeps counting, `status` stays `KNOWN`. Demotion is the same rule running backwards and needs no special case. Putting `kind` in the key would remember one bug twice and list it twice.
   - **The merge is idempotent.** It always reads the pre-scan photocopy plus everything this scan has found so far, so `scans` rises by exactly 1 however many times it runs inside one scan. "Have I already counted this key?" is a question that cannot arise. Where one key appears more than once in `scan-rows.tsv`, the last row wins — which is what makes a Lead proven by a later pass land as `FINDING`.

   c. **Move it into place.**

   ```bash
   mv .solidity-auditor/memory.tsv.tmp .solidity-auditor/memory.tsv
   ```

   The temporary file sits beside the real one so the move stays on one disk. **The new file is always written before the old one is replaced** — an interrupted scan leaves one whole ledger, never half of one. Never write `memory.tsv` directly.

   `mkdir -p .solidity-auditor` before the first write. The user is expected to gitignore that directory; the ledger is not shared between machines or people.

   **Then write the other two `mem_` keys**, every pass, immediately after the move:

   ```bash
   printf '%s\t%s\n' mem_after "$(( $(wc -l < .solidity-auditor/memory.tsv) - 1 ))" \
     >> .solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/scope.tsv
   printf '%s\t%s\n' mem_sha "$(git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo none)" \
     >> .solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/scope.tsv
   ```

   Both are re-written on every pass and **last wins**, so the `Memory` row ends up describing the ledger as the scan left it, with no delete step and no "have I written this already?" flag. `mem_before` is not touched here — it was written once, in Turn 2 step 2c, and the row's arithmetic depends on it staying put.

   d. **In a loop, this step runs after every pass, and it rebuilds rather than appends.** Pass K+1 learns what pass K found by reading the merged ledger, so the write cannot wait for the end. But re-running the merge N times must not raise `scans` by N, because `scans` counts scans. The command above already holds this: it always reads the **pre-scan photocopy** plus **everything this scan has accumulated so far**, so `scans` rises by exactly 1 however many passes ran. Nothing new is invented per pass, and no "have I counted this key already?" flag exists to get wrong. It also keeps the interrupt rule for the whole loop: a loop killed at pass 3 keeps what passes 1 and 2 learned, written atomically.

   Then the next pass starts at **Turn 2 step 2c**, which rebuilds `known-findings.md` from the freshly merged `.solidity-auditor/memory.tsv` — not from the photocopy, or pass K+1 would never see pass K's findings — and re-cats the twelve bundles at Turn 2 step 3.

## Turn 5

**Turn 5 — Assemble, print, clean.** Runs **once per scan**, at any pass count, including a 1-pass scan and including a loop that stopped early. There is no path where a scan ends without this turn.

> **This turn no longer composes a report, and must never be re-taught to.** It used to combine the runs, dedup them, build the "Known from earlier scans" rows and format the whole thing — all of it model work, all of it at the moment of least remaining context. On a real 3-pass scan that produced 71 findings, it printed 14 of them in full, collapsed the rest into two lines, and **claimed a coverage it did not have**. Nothing was lost from disk; the report lied about what it was showing. A prose instruction cannot fix that, because the orchestrator under context pressure is the thing that failed.
>
> So the step that must not lose a finding holds **no model judgment**. The dedup, the `seen in k/N runs` counts, the strongest-kind rule, the "Known from earlier scans" rows and the whole report body are `assemble.sh`'s work now, and it is shell. This turn copies two files, runs it, counts, and prints. If you are reading this turn and it looks too thin to be a reporting step — that is the point.

1. **Copy the memory inputs in.** **SKIP when memory is off.** The assembler reads one directory, so anything it needs that lives in `{bundle_dir}` has to be in the runs directory before it runs:

   ```bash
   cp {bundle_dir}/memory-before.tsv {bundle_dir}/source-names.tsv .solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/
   ```

   `memory-before.tsv` is the **pruned** photocopy — the "Known from earlier scans" section is built from it, so a record the prune dropped must not reappear here. `source-names.tsv` turns a normalised key back into the spelling the source uses, so no reader is ever shown `gatewaytransfernative.withdrawtonativechain`.

   Only these two. `run-keys.tsv` and `scan-rows.tsv` are **not** copied: the keys this scan raised come from the assembler's own index of the run files, which is the same data with no copy step.

2. **Assemble the report.**

   ```bash
   bash {resolved_path}/assemble.sh --dir .solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}
   ```

   It writes `.solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/full-report.md` — the whole report, banner line down to the disclaimer, ready to print word for word. It writes to a `.part` file and moves it into place, so a half-report never exists.

   **This is the only producer of a report in this skill.** Do not re-word its output, do not re-order it, do not add to it and do not summarise it in your own words. Do not re-read source to "verify the most critical claim" either — the agents did that and the gate filtered it; re-verification costs about five minutes and rarely changes a verdict.

   If it exits non-zero, print its stderr and stop. It has told you it could not read its own inputs, and there is nothing for a model to salvage by hand.

3. **Count the findings, then branch.** One `awk` over the assembled file, no model arithmetic anywhere:

   ```bash
   awk '
   /^## Leads$/  { sec="leads"; next }
   /^## /        { sec="";      next }
   /^\[[0-9]+\]/ { F++; next }
   sec=="leads" && /^- \*\*/ { L++ }
   /Confidence: [0-9]+/ && /^`/ {
     match($0, /Confidence: [0-9]+/)
     c = substr($0, RSTART+12, RLENGTH-12) + 0
     if (c >= 90) A++; else if (c >= 75) B++; else C++
   }
   END { printf "%d %d %d %d %d\n", F, L, A, B, C }
   ' .solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/full-report.md
   ```

   `F` is findings, `L` leads, and `A` / `B` / `C` the confidence buckets `100-90`, `89-75` and `below 75`.

   **Only `F` is printed** — it is the trigger and it is the total in `top 3 of {F}`. `L`, `A`, `B` and `C` are computed anyway and kept as a **self-check**, not as output.

   > **`A + B + C` must equal `F`.** The buckets are the whole set, in every mode. If they do not sum, the assembled file is malformed — a finding block the counter could not read is a finding block a reader may not get either. Say so and print the full report rather than a three-row slice of a file you cannot stand behind.

   **The trigger is more than 20 findings** — `F` alone. Leads are excluded, so a scan with 18 findings and 40 leads still prints in full.

   a. **`F` is 20 or fewer — print `full-report.md` word for word.** Every byte, nothing added, nothing cut, no preface. This is the path a plain scan of a small contract takes, and its printed bytes are exactly what this skill printed before any of this existed.

   b. **`F` is above 20 — print this instead**, and nothing else:

   ````markdown
   # 🔐 Security Review — {project-name}

   ---

   ## Scope

   {the Scope table from full-report.md, copied unchanged}

   ---

   Findings List — top 3 of {F}

   | # | Confidence | Title | Location | Seen |
   |---|---|---|---|---|
   {the three rows the extractor below printed}

   **→ Full findings list, every description and every fix:** {path}

   ---

   > ⚠️ {the disclaimer line from full-report.md, copied unchanged}
   ````

   - **`{path}`** — `.solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/full-report.md`, or, when `--file-output` was passed, the **copy** and only the copy: `{project-name}-pashov-ai-audit-report-{stamp}.md`. Never both. Two paths to identical bytes answers a question the runner did not ask at the moment they want one filename. This line is the only part of the block a flag changes.
   - **The Scope table's `Files reviewed` row is copied unchanged**, full paths and all. It is the one row that proves *which* `SafeMath.sol` was read, and a terminal that shortens it can no longer be diffed against the file it claims to summarise.
   - **No counts summary.** The `{F} findings, {L} leads` line and the `100-90 / 89-75 / below 75` split are **not** printed. `top 3 of {F}` already carries the only total a reader needs at this moment, and the bucket split answered a question nobody asked while standing between them and the path.

   > **The `{F}` in `top 3 of {F}` is what makes the slice safe, and it is not optional.** The rule this block obeys is that a report may print **less** than the scan found and may never look like it printed **more**. A bare list of three findings breaks that rule — a reader cannot tell a truncated list from a complete one. `top 3 of 52` cannot be misread, and it sits in the header rather than in a footnote for exactly that reason. An editor who drops the total, or moves it below the table, has re-created the failure this sentence exists to prevent.
   >
   > **This replaces the older "nothing is enumerated above the trigger" rule.** That rule was right about bare truncation and wrong to conclude that no slice can ever be honest; a counted slice is. Still enumerated **nowhere**: the Leads section, the "Known from earlier scans" section, and findings 4 and beyond. Three rows, and the header says three.

   **The three rows are extracted by shell, never typed from memory.** The orchestrator has by this point read dozens of findings and is the least reliable thing in the room; one `awk` over the assembled file cannot mis-rank, mis-quote a function name or invent a confidence. Pass `-v withseen=1` when the `Passes` row is printed — that is, when `{passes}` is above 1 — and `0` otherwise, because a plain scan's location line carries no `seen in k/N runs` and an empty column would print as a stub:

   ```bash
   awk -v withseen={1 or 0} '
   /^\[[0-9]+\] \*\*/ {
     if (n >= 3) exit
     line = $0
     match(line, /^\[[0-9]+\]/); conf = substr(line, RSTART+1, RLENGTH-2)
     sub(/^\[[0-9]+\] \*\*[0-9]+\. /, "", line); sub(/\*\*[ \t]*$/, "", line)
     title = line; want = 1; next
   }
   want && /^`/ {
     loc = $0
     match(loc, /^`[^`]*`/); fn = substr(loc, RSTART+1, RLENGTH-2)
     n++
     if (withseen) {
       seen = ""
       if (match(loc, /seen in [0-9]+\/[0-9]+ runs/)) seen = substr(loc, RSTART+8, RLENGTH-13)
       printf "| %d | [%s] | %s | `%s` | %s |\n", n, conf, title, fn, seen
     } else printf "| %d | [%s] | %s | `%s` |\n", n, conf, title, fn
     want = 0
   }
   ' .solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/full-report.md
   ```

   With `withseen=0` the awk prints four columns, so **drop `Seen` from the header row and from the separator row too** — a five-column header over four-column rows renders as a broken table in every terminal that draws one.

   The assembled file is already sorted highest-confidence first, so "top 3" is the first three finding blocks and no sort happens here. `exit` after the third block means the extractor does not read the rest of the file.

   **Fewer than 3 findings cannot reach this branch** — `F` is above 20 or this block is not printed — so the extractor needs no short-list case.

4. **`--file-output` — copy the assembled file.** Only when the flag was passed:

   ```bash
   cp .solidity-auditor/runs/{stamp}/full-report.md "{project-name}-pashov-ai-audit-report-{stamp}.md"
   ```

   A copy, not a second build. **Nothing regenerates**, so the flag cannot collapse the report the way the terminal once did — the file and the terminal are the same bytes by construction, whatever the finding count. The run files stay in `.solidity-auditor/runs/` and are never copied into the working directory.

5. **Auto-clean.** `rm -rf {bundle_dir}`. Bundle dir = transient build state, not an artifact. Don't skip. It runs once per scan, at any pass count, and it runs when the loop stopped early too. For debugging a loop: copy the bundle elsewhere before re-running.

   > **It runs last, and the order is load-bearing.** Step 1 copies two files **out of** `{bundle_dir}`, and step 2 reads them. Deleting the bundle before either has run destroys the "Known from earlier scans" section and the name map that keeps it readable — silently, because the assembler treats a missing input as an absent section and carries on. Steps 1 → 2 → 5 is not a style preference; moving this step earlier breaks a report that will still look finished.

   Do **not** add a per-pass partial clean — reclaiming disk between passes would mean rebuilding `source.md`, the one thing built once. Do **not** add a startup sweep of stale `.audit-*` directories: a crashed scan leaks one, as it does today, and a sweep would delete the working directory of a second scan running at the same time on the same repo.

[Feynman: Distribution.init] When the factory makes a new copy, it calls this once. It records the owner, the waiting time and the description, and stores the list of who gets paid. It works only if the caller is the factory and no list exists yet. The implementation's own copy has the factory as its deployer, but the factory never calls `init` on it. Every successful `init` writes a non-empty list, so a second call fails.

[Inversion: Distribution.init] (1) An attacker calls `init` on the implementation directly. It fails because `msg.sender != factory`. (2) An attacker calls `init` on a fresh clone before the factory does. It fails because `create` runs create2 and `init` in the same transaction, and the caller check still applies. (3) An attacker gets the factory to call `init` on an existing clone. It fails because create2 reverts first, with `DeploymentFailed`.

[Feynman: Distribution.propose / applyQueued / cancel] The owner writes down a change. If the wait is zero, the change runs now. If not, the change becomes due after the wait. Once it is due, anyone may run it for 14 days. After that, anyone may delete it. The owner may delete it at any time. The change runs as a call from the contract to itself, which is the only way to reach the setters.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:245 — why can anyone call applyQueued?] The design wants "permissionless execution". The belief underneath is that the owner never cares when, or in what order, matured actions run. That belief is untested. Compound's admin-only execute does not rest on it.

[Inversion: applyQueued] (1) A non-owner applies an action before it matures. `NotReady` stops this. (2) A non-owner changes the calldata. The hash binds both `action` and `nonce_`. (3) A non-owner applies two matured `setBeneficiaries` actions in the reverse order. Nothing stops this. That is the lead below.

[Feynman: transferOwnership / acceptOwnership] The owner names a successor, and the successor must accept. Accepting, or renouncing, deletes every waiting change. Renouncing clears the successor too.

[Inversion: acceptOwnership] (1) Someone calls it while `pendingOwner == 0`. `msg.sender` is never zero, so it fails. (2) The pending owner, as a beneficiary, accepts during `distribute`. This changes only `owner` and the queue, not `_table`, so the payout does not change. (3) The owner names `address(this)`, and then a self-call accepts. Ownership locks, but only the owner can do this to themselves.

[Feynman: distribute / release / claim] `distribute` splits the unreserved balance across the list. Any push that fails goes into a per-account escrow. `release` lets anyone retry one escrow, with capped gas. `claim` lets the escrowed account send its own escrow anywhere. All three take the lock. `propose` and `applyQueued` refuse to run while the lock is held. `cancel` and `acceptOwnership` do not, and neither one touches the table.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:379 — what can a self-call reach?] Every external function. `claim` through a self-call reads `escrowed[token][address(this)]`. That entry is the contract's own money, so a self-call takes nothing that belongs to a beneficiary. `init` fails because the contract is not the factory.

[Feynman: DistributionFactory.create] The function puts a minimal copy at an address that depends only on the factory and the salt. The salt's top 20 bytes must equal the caller, so only that caller can claim the address. The owner, the list and the description are not part of the address.

[Inversion: create] (1) An attacker front-runs with the victim's salt. The prefix check stops this. (2) An attacker pre-funds the address. The money is logged at `init` and paid out under the victim's list. (3) The same sender address has a different holder on another chain, for example a Safe, or a deployer key that leaked. That holder can create the "same" clone with its own list. That is the lead below.

[Feynman: App] The owner adds or sets stored chunks of the page, then locks it. Locking checks that every pointer has code that starts with 0x00. Such code cannot run, so it cannot change or destroy itself. After the lock, every setter reverts.

[Inversion: App.lock] (1) Point at a 7702-delegated EOA. Its code starts with `0xef`, so `ForeignChunk` rejects it. (2) Point at an empty address that gets code later. `CodelessChunk` rejects it at lock time. (3) Point at a contract that starts with 0x00 and later uses SELFDESTRUCT. It cannot run any opcode, so it cannot. I found no gap. The other owner-only setters all check `locked`.

[Feynman: Deploy scripts] The factory and `App` are placed with CREATE2 through Arachnid's deployer. Anyone who copies the deploy gets the same contract, with the same owner baked in. That causes no harm.

code_smells: `applyQueued` has no caller check, so a third party chooses when and in what order matured actions run during the `GRACE` window. Compound's Timelock limits `executeTransaction` to the admin. Example: the owner queues `setBeneficiaries(T2)` at nonce 1 and `setBeneficiaries(T3)` at nonce 2 to replace it, but does not cancel nonce 1. Once both mature, a beneficiary of T2 calls `applyQueued(T3,2)` and then `applyQueued(T2,1)`, so `_table` ends as T2. The same caller can also put `applyQueued` before or after `distribute` to pick which table pays the current balance.
description: Any caller can apply matured actions in any order. We did not confirm that an owner leaves two conflicting actions queued without a cancel.

LEAD | contract: DistributionFactory | function: create | bug_class: unbound-clone-config | group_key: DistributionFactory | create | unbound-clone-config
code_smells: The clone address is `keccak(0xff, factory, salt, initCodeHash)`, and the only check is `salt >> 96 == msg.sender`. `owner_` and `table_` do not enter the address. Trace: E creates clone X on chain A with owner = Vault and table = T. Funds reach X on chain B before anyone deploys there. Whoever controls address E on chain B (a leaked "disposable" deploy key, or a different Safe at the same address) calls `create(E, 0, "", [{E,10000}], salt)`. `init` accepts the balance, and `distribute` pays it all to E. The NatSpec documents this as design ("the owner does not enter it"), and the attacker must control the sender address.
description: The holder of the deployer address on a new chain can deploy the shared clone address with its own owner and table. That holder then takes the funds already sent there.
fix: Mix `keccak256(abi.encode(owner_, delay_, description_, table_))` into the CREATE2 salt in `create` and `predict`.

- `init` cannot be taken over, on the implementation or on a clone.
- Every setter is `onlySelf`, and the timelock is the only way to reach them.
- `cancel` and `acceptOwnership` are open during a lock, but neither changes `_table`.
- The swap-and-pop in `_remove` and `_clearQueue` keep `_pendingIndex` consistent.
- `App`'s setters all check `locked`, and `_requireChunk` correctly rejects code that is empty or starts with `0xef`.

[Feynman: receive] When a clone gets plain ETH with no call data, it hands the call to the shared implementation code, which checks it is not running as the implementation and writes a log. The fuzzy point is "hands the call to". A clone pays to reach the implementation's code, and the comment at Distribution.sol:149 promises this works on a 2,300-gas budget.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:149 — why?] Why can it run on 2,300 gas? The body (one compare and one LOG2, about 1,400 gas) fits. The belief under it is that the DELEGATECALL from the clone to the implementation is cheap. Under EIP-2929 the first touch of an address in a transaction costs 2,600 gas, which is more than the whole stipend.

[Inversion: receive] (1) A seller contract calls `payable(dist).transfer(1 ether)` in a fresh transaction. The implementation is cold, so the clone runs out of gas. (2) A payer uses `send` and ignores the result. The ETH stays with the payer and nothing logs it. (3) A payer that adds the implementation to an access list gets through. This shows the failure comes from gas cost, not from the guard.

[Feynman: distribute] It works out what the contract holds beyond money already owed to failed recipients, then pays each table row its share in order. Any failed payment goes into escrow. The ETH payments are capped at 100k gas. The ERC-20 payments forward all gas.

[Inversion: distribute] (1) A caller gives a small gas limit so a Safe recipient fails. 63/64 forwarding means the escrow writes cannot then succeed, so the whole call reverts and nothing changes. (2) A recipient returns megabytes of data on the ETH path. Output size 0 means the contract never copies it. (3) A hook recipient on an ERC-777-style token burns all forwarded gas. Only 1/64 of the gas comes back, so the rest of the loop runs out of gas. This one is unguarded (LEAD below).

[Feynman: propose / applyQueued / cancel / _remove / _clearQueue] The owner queues calldata that the contract calls on itself. Anyone can apply it between the eta and eta+GRACE. The owner can cancel at any time, and anyone can cancel after expiry. The swap-and-pop keeps the index map consistent. I found no path to apply an unqueued hash: `queued` is written only in `propose`, and the hash commits to the nonce.

[Feynman: DistributionFactory.create / predict] The salt prefix must equal the sender, so nobody else can take your address. The init-code bytes match solady `initCode_PUSH0`. The free memory pointer bytes 0x40–0x43 are restored to zero, and they were zero before.

[Feynman: App._requireChunk / lock] Code that starts with 0x00 stops at once and can never run SELFDESTRUCT. Code that starts with 0xef (a 7702 designator) is refused. A pointer that passes the check therefore cannot change after lock. Nothing except `transferOwnership` stays mutable after `lock`.

[Inversion: _requireChunk] (1) A codeless address that someone deploys later is rejected as CodelessChunk. (2) A 7702 EOA is rejected as ForeignChunk. (3) A metamorphic CREATE2 contract with a 0x00 prefix cannot self-destruct, because it can never run an opcode. The check holds.

Deploy scripts: re-deploying the factory or App at the same address on another chain gives the same code and the same owner, so it does no harm. The comment at Distribution.sol:457 says the factory is "nonce-addressed", but Deploy.s.sol uses CREATE2. That is only a stale comment.

---

path: payer contract → payable(clone).transfer(x) / send(x) (2,300 stipend) → clone runtime DELEGATECALL to cold implementation → OOG → payer reverts (transfer) or keeps the ETH with no log (send)
proof: Clone runtime 0x365f5f37365f73<impl>5af4... runs CALLDATASIZE, PUSH0, PUSH0, CALLDATACOPY(size 0), CALLDATASIZE, PUSH0, PUSH20, GAS = 18 gas, then DELEGATECALL. EIP-2929 cold access cost = 2,600 > 2,300 - 18 = 2,282 available, so the call fails before any implementation code runs. When the implementation is warm (access list or earlier touch), the body is about 100 + dispatch + LOG2(375+2*375+8*32 = 1,381) and fits. So the comment at Distribution.sol:149 ("Must run under a 2,300-gas `transfer` stipend") holds only when the implementation is warm, and in a normal transaction it is cold.

fix: Make the clone handle empty calldata itself with a LOG2 and a STOP before the DELEGATECALL, or remove the 2,300-gas promise and document that `transfer` payers fail.

A hook that loops to OOG leaves only 1/64 of the gas to the loop: 30M → about 470k after one row, too little for up to 106 more rows and their escrow writes.

- **Finding: `Distribution.receive`.** A payer that uses `transfer` or `send` cannot pay a clone, because the clone's first DELEGATECALL to the cold implementation costs 2,600 gas, more than the 2,300-gas stipend. The opcode costs in the proof block show this. The comment at `/home/openclaw/src/rake-blind-2026-11-02/src/Distribution.sol:149` assumes the call fits in the stipend, and it fits only when the implementation is warm.
- **Lead: `Distribution._push`, ERC-20 branch.** This branch has no gas cap. A beneficiary on a token with recipient hooks can use up the gas so that `distribute` reverts. I did not check which tokens in scope call such hooks.

These paths held, with no finding:
- The timelock (`propose`, `applyQueued`, `cancel`, `_remove`, `_clearQueue`).
- The ownership handover.
- The factory init code and its memory restore in `create` and `predict`.
- The salt prefix check, which stops address squatting.
- `App._requireChunk` and `lock`, so a locked chunk cannot change.
- Both deploy scripts.

One stale comment at `/home/openclaw/src/rake-blind-2026-11-02/src/Distribution.sol:457` says the factory is "nonce-addressed", but `/home/openclaw/src/rake-blind-2026-11-02/scripts/forge/Deploy.s.sol` places it with CREATE2. It is not a security issue.

[Feynman: Distribution.distribute] Anyone can call it. It splits every unreserved token or ETH balance across the table by bps, and the last row gets the remainder. A failed push goes into escrow for that account and adds to `reserved`.

[Feynman: Distribution.release / claim] These are the pair that pays escrow out. `release` lets anyone retry the push to the account, with a gas cap for ETH. `claim` lets the account itself take its escrow to any `to`, with no gas cap. Both set the escrow to zero and lower `reserved` before the call, and both hold the lock.

[Feynman: Distribution.propose / applyQueued / cancel] The owner queues a self-call keyed by `keccak(action, nonce)`. Anyone applies it between eta and eta+GRACE. The owner cancels it at any time, and anyone cancels it after GRACE.

[Feynman: transferOwnership / acceptOwnership] Two-step handover, or renounce at once. Both the accept and the renounce clear the queue.

[Feynman: DistributionFactory.create / predict] Makes a PUSH0 clone with CREATE2. The salt's top 20 bytes must equal the sender, then the factory calls `init`.

[Feynman: App] The owner stores SSTORE2 chunks. `lock` checks that each pointer is a real chunk (has code, first byte 0x00) and then freezes it.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:121 — why does `notLocked` guard only `propose` and `applyQueued`?] The code assumes that only an `onlySelf` mutator changes configuration. But `acceptOwnership` and `cancel` also change governance state, and they have no guard.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:158 — why is `amount = _balance(token) - reserved[token]` correct?] It assumes that one token address maps to one balance and that the balance moves only by transfer. A token with two entry addresses, or a rebasing token, breaks that.

[Inversion: distribute ETH gas-starvation] Move 1: the caller sets the gas so that row k's push gets less than 100k. EIP-150 then gives the call 63/64 of what is left, and the remaining 1/64 cannot pay for the escrow SSTOREs (about 45k), so the whole tx reverts. The caller cannot force a selected escrow. Move 2: a recipient burns its 100k and reverts. Its own share goes to escrow and the loop continues. Move 3: a recipient sends megabytes of revert data. The assembly call has a zero-length output area. All three fail.

[Inversion: applyQueued self-call] Move 1: `action = distribute(t)`. It takes the lock itself, so this is harmless. Move 2: `action = claim(t, owner)`. It moves only `escrowed[t][address(this)]`, and the owner could take that by a table change anyway. Move 3: `action = propose(...)`. It fails `NotOwner`. All fail.

[Inversion: cancel boundary] At `t == eta+GRACE`, `applyQueued` works and a non-owner `cancel` reverts. At `t == eta+GRACE+1`, the reverse is true. The two checks are consistent.

[Inversion: App._requireChunk] An EIP-7702 designator starts with 0xef, so `lock` rejects it. Precompiles have no code, so it rejects them too. A contract whose code starts with STOP halts at pc 0, so it cannot run SELFDESTRUCT. All fail.

[Inversion: factory salt] Another sender cannot use my salt prefix. If someone deploys the factory first through Arachnid, the factory at that address has the same bytecode and no owner, so nothing is lost.

code_smells: `amount = _balance(token) - reserved[token]` reads a balance from the token but subtracts a reserve kept per token address; a rebase on the reserved part also goes to the whole table.
description: A double-entry token or a rebasing token makes `distribute` pay out escrowed tokens, so a later `release` or `claim` fails. We did not find a live token in scope.
```

```
LEAD | contract: Distribution | function: acceptOwnership | bug_class: missing-notLocked-guard | group_key: Distribution | acceptOwnership | missing-notLocked-guard
code_smells: `propose` and `applyQueued` carry `notLocked` for the reason "a configuration change landing between two rows of `distribute`", but `acceptOwnership` and `cancel` have no guard; a `pendingOwner` that is also a beneficiary can call `acceptOwnership` from its ETH push and replace `owner` and clear `_pending` in the middle of `distribute`.
description: A pending owner who is also a beneficiary can take ownership and clear the queue during `distribute`. We found no path from this to a change in the table or the payouts.
```

code_smells: `_clearQueue` pops every `_pending` entry and its `bytes action` storage in one loop, with no cap on how many entries `propose` can add.

content.text:
I found one confirmed finding. I also traced the other boundaries and found no second exploitable path.

[Feynman: Distribution.receive] When someone sends plain ETH to a split contract, the contract writes a log entry that names the sender and the amount. It must do this with the 2,300 gas that `transfer`/`send` pass along. Each split contract is a small forwarding stub, and the stub passes every call on to the shared implementation. The fuzzy spot: the comment counts only the cost of the log. It leaves out the cost of the forwarding.

[Socratic: src/Distribution.sol:149 — why "must run under a 2,300-gas stipend"?] Because payers that use `transfer` or `send` forward only 2,300 gas. Does that budget pay for the stub's DELEGATECALL into the implementation? Under EIP-2929 a cold DELEGATECALL costs 2,600, which is more than 2,300. The code assumes the forwarding is free, and it is not.

[Inversion: DistributionFactory.create / receive] (1) A contract pays the clone with `payable(clone).transfer(1 ether)` in a fresh transaction. Result: OutOfGas, so the payment reverts. (2) The same payment with `send` returns false. (3) The same payment works only after something in the same transaction touches the implementation address, which a normal payer never does.

```
FINDING | contract: DistributionFactory | function: create | bug_class: stipend-cold-delegatecall | group_key: DistributionFactory | create | stipend-cold-delegatecall
boundary: the 2,300-gas stipend call from `transfer`/`send` into a PUSH0 minimal-proxy clone, which then runs DELEGATECALL into `implementation` before `Distribution.receive`
assumption: src/Distribution.sol:149 says "Must run under a 2,300-gas `transfer` stipend", so the code expects `transfer`/`send` payers to be able to pay a clone
actual: the clone's runtime (`...73<impl>5af4...`) runs DELEGATECALL to a cold `implementation` (2,600 gas under EIP-2929) before any of `receive` runs, so the call runs out of gas
path: payer contract → payable(clone).transfer(v) → clone stub → DELEGATECALL impl (cold, 2600 > 2300) → OutOfGas → transfer reverts / send returns false → the Distribution never receives the ETH
proof: scratch Foundry project at /tmp/poc9 (not in the audited repo), with the src copied, evm_version cancun, via_ir. Payer.payTransfer{value: 1 ether}(clone) traces as "[2300] clone::receive{value: 1e18}() ← [OutOfGas]", so test_transfer FAILs; Payer.paySend returns false, so test_send FAILs. Control test: WarmPayer reads `impl.code.length` first to warm the address, then the same `transfer` PASSes and clone.balance == 1 ether. This shows that the cold DELEGATECALL is the cause.
description: A clone rejects every `transfer` or `send` payment, because its stub spends 2,600 gas on a cold DELEGATECALL before `receive` runs, and the stipend is 2,300.
fix: Give the clone runtime a code path that emits the `Received` log and stops when calldata is empty, without DELEGATECALL; or deploy full `Distribution` contracts in place of proxies.
```

Impact notes for the caller:
- Any payer that uses `transfer` reverts. Examples are older royalty or marketplace payout code and some exchange withdrawals.
- A payer that uses `send` gets false. If that payer ignores the return value, it counts the beneficiary as paid but keeps the ETH.
- No funds already in a Distribution are at risk. The defect stops payments from arriving, and it makes the NatSpec promise at line 149 false.

Boundaries I checked and found safe:
- **Tokens with no code:** `_balance` reverts on empty return data, so `distribute` cannot run for such a token.
- **Odd token addresses:** precompile or hostile "tokens" stay in their own `escrowed`/`reserved` entries.
- **Reentry during a money path:** `cancel` and `acceptOwnership` are not lock-guarded, but they move no funds and cannot change the table in the middle of a loop.
- **Gas starvation to force escrow:** this does not work. The 63/64 rule leaves too little gas for the escrow SSTOREs.
- **Factory memory writes:** the `create`/`predict` assembly restores the free memory pointer, as solady does.
- **`App._requireChunk`:** it rejects empty-code and 0xef (EIP-7702) pointers correctly.
- **Deploy scripts:** I found no issue.

The PoC is in /tmp/poc9/test/Stipend.t.sol. Nothing in /home/openclaw/src/rake-blind-2026-11-02 changed. The audited tree has no `test/` directory, so I could not check whether the project's own tests cover the stipend.

content.text: Agent 6 (periphery) returned 1 finding and 1 lead. The finding: a clone's first DELEGATECALL to the cold implementation costs 2,600 gas, more than the 2,300-gas stipend, so a payer that uses `transfer` or `send` cannot pay a clone. I checked it against EIP-2929 and it holds. Waiting for the other 7.

[Feynman: Distribution.distribute] The contract takes everything it holds of one token, minus the money it already holds back for failed payees. It pays each row its share of that amount, rounded down. The last row gets whatever is left. If a payment fails, the money stays in the contract, and the contract records it as owed to that row (`escrowed`) and as held back in total (`reserved`). The fuzzy spot: "everything it holds minus the held-back total" assumes the balance never falls below `reserved` unless this contract sends money out.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:158 — why?] Why is `_balance(token) - reserved[token]` safe? Because every path that raises `reserved` keeps the same tokens in the contract. Why is that enough? It is only enough if the token's balance cannot fall on its own. Nothing checks that.

[Inversion: distribute rounding] (1) Call `distribute` after every 1-wei deposit. Every row except the last gets 0, and the last row (the highest address) gets 1 wei. (2) Use a 2-decimal token and amount = 9,999. A 1-bps row gets 0 and loses at most 1 unit. (3) Make `bps * amount` overflow, which needs a balance above about 1.15e73 of a token the attacker controls. All three are rounding dust or self-harm, so I dropped them.

[Inversion: distribute gas starvation] To make row k's capped ETH push fail while the rest of the loop still runs, the attacker needs `63/64·g < X` and `g/64 > R`. Here X ≤ `PUSH_GAS` = 100,000, and R ≥ about 45,000 (two cold SSTOREs for the escrow, plus the event). So X > 63·R ≈ 2.8M, which the cap does not allow. The attack fails. The ERC-20 branch has no cap, so I checked it separately (Lead 2).

[Feynman: release / claim] Anyone can retry a held payment with the capped gas. The payee itself can take its own held money to any address and pay its own gas. Both lower `escrowed` and `reserved` before they send.

[Feynman: propose / applyQueued / cancel] The owner queues a call to this contract. After the delay, anyone can run it for 14 days. After that, anyone can drop it. [Feynman: Distribution] One clone holds money for a fixed list of payees. Anyone can tell it to split its balance among them, minus money it already holds back for payees whose payments failed. If a payment to a payee fails, the clone keeps that payee's share aside, and the payee or anyone else can retry it later. Every change to the list, the owner, the delay or the description must wait in a public queue for a set time. Fuzzy spot: "anything else must answer with a word", because the ERC-20 branch forwards all gas and copies all return data. The comment assumes that only the token can harm this call, but some tokens call the payee during the transfer.

[Feynman: distribute] It takes the balance, subtracts what it holds back, and pays each row its share in order. The last row gets the remainder. A failed payment is set aside instead of stopping the loop. For ETH, each call to a payee gets at most 100k gas and copies no return data. For ERC-20, the call to the token gets all the gas, and the clone copies every byte the token returns.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:420 — why does the ERC-20 call have no gas cap and no limit on return data?] The answer is "the token is the caller's choice." That rests on a belief: the token's behaviour depends only on the token. A hook token (ERC-777 `tokensReceived`) breaks that belief, because it runs payee code inside the token call.

[Inversion: distribute ERC-20 branch] (1) A payee's hook burns all the gas it gets, so the clone keeps about 1/32 of the gas for the rows that follow. (2) A payee's hook burns gas down to R, then reverts with S bytes. The token can afford to copy S, but the clone, with its 1/64 share, cannot, so the whole tx runs out of gas. (3) A payee's hook reverts with nothing, so the share is held back for that payee. That only harms the payee.

[Feynman: propose/applyQueued/cancel] The owner queues a call to itself. After the delay, anyone can run it for 14 days. The owner can cancel it at any time, and anyone can cancel it after it expires. If the delay is zero, the call runs at once.

[Inversion: transferOwnership withdrawal] (1) The owner names B, then queues `transferOwnership(owner)` to undo it, and B calls `acceptOwnership` before that call is due. This clears the queue, so the undo never runs. (2) The owner tries `setDelay(0)` first, but that also waits for the delay. (3) The owner calls `cancel`, but nothing is left to cancel, because the nomination already ran.

[Feynman: DistributionFactory.create] The sender owns a salt that starts with its own address. The clone address depends only on the factory and the salt. The sender then picks any owner and any list.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:448 — why must the owner not enter the address?] So that one address works on every chain. The hidden belief is that the person who holds the salt is harmless. But on any chain where no clone exists yet, the salt holder alone picks who gets the money already sent to that address.

[Feynman: _balance / reserved] The money it holds back is counted per token address. The amount to share is the balance minus that count.

[Inversion: distribute amount] (1) A token whose balance can fall (rebasing, seizure) drops below `reserved`, so the subtraction reverts. (2) A token with two entry addresses: `reserved[B]` is 0, so a split through B pays out what is held back for A. (3) The last row calls `distribute` after every small deposit and collects the rounding remainder.

[Feynman: App] The owner stores web pages in data contracts and serves them. Locking freezes the list of pointers. `_requireChunk` refuses pointers with no code and pointers whose first byte is not 00. A pointer that starts with 00 halts at once, so its code cannot change. [Inversion: App.lock] (1) A 7702 pointer starts with 0xef and is refused. (2) A pointer with no code yet is refused. (3) A pointer that starts with 00 cannot run SELFDESTRUCT. I found no path.

[Feynman: Deploy scripts] They put the factory and App at fixed addresses through the CREATE2 deployer. App's address depends on OWNER and the version. I found no exploitable issue.

Report summary:
- **Main finding (Distribution.distribute):** for tokens that call the receiver during a transfer (ERC-777 style), the ERC-20 transfer passes on all gas and copies all return data. One hostile beneficiary can then make `distribute(token)` fail for every caller until the owner removes that row through the timelock.
- **Second finding (DistributionFactory.create/predict):** the clone address depends only on the factory and the salt, not on the settings. So the salt holder decides the table on every chain where no clone exists yet, and takes any funds already sent to that address there.
- **Leads:** the owner cannot take back a nomination, because the withdrawal waits for the timelock and the nominee's accept clears it from the queue. The other two leads are a token balance that falls below `reserved` (or a token with two addresses), and rounding that favours the last row.
- I found nothing exploitable in App.sol or the deploy scripts.

[Feynman: Distribution] A clone holds ETH and tokens for a group of payees. Anyone can tell it to split its free balance by fixed percentages. A payee that cannot take its share has the share held for it. One owner changes the setup, and each change must wait in a queue for a set time. Fuzzy spot: who may *finish* a queued change? The code lets anyone run it, not only the owner.

[Feynman: DistributionFactory.create] The caller picks a salt whose top 20 bytes are the caller's own address. The factory places a clone at an address that comes only from the factory and the salt. Then it sets the owner, delay and payee table that the caller passes. Fuzzy spot: the address does not depend on the owner or the table, so one address can carry different owners on different chains.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:448 — why does the address leave out the owner?] So that one EOA can reach the same address on every chain with a different vault owner on each. → What does the code assume? That only the honest deploy of the salt key is ever made, on every chain, for all time. → What if the key acts later, or someone takes the key? Then the key holder sets any owner and table on any chain where the clone is not yet deployed.

[Inversion: DistributionFactory.create]
1. The salt-key holder waits until a bridge or exchange sends 10 ETH to the known address on chain B, which has no clone yet. Then the holder calls `create(self, 0, "", [{self,10000}], salt)`.
2. The holder deploys the factory on chain B through Arachnid's deployer. Anyone can do this, and the factory lands at the same address because the bytecode is the same. The holder then creates the clone with a hostile table.
3. A front-runner without the key cannot do it, because the prefix check stops them. The only path is the key holder, now or after a key leak.

[Feynman: distribute] It takes the token balance minus the amounts held for failed payees. It pays each row its share, and the last row gets the remainder. A failed push becomes a held amount. Anyone can call it at any time.

[Inversion: distribute]
1. The caller gives just enough gas that an ETH push runs out of gas. The push gets at least 100k gas unless less than about 101.6k is left, and then 1/64 of that (about 1.6k) cannot pay for the two stores that hold the share, so the whole call reverts. No gain.
2. A beneficiary with an ERC-777 `tokensReceived` hook uses up all the gas on a token push. That push has no gas cap, so `distribute(token)` reverts for every caller (LEAD 2).
3. The token balance drops below `reserved` through a rebase, so `_balance - reserved` underflows (LEAD 3).

[Feynman: applyQueued] Anyone runs a matured queued action, at any moment within 14 days after its eta.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:245 — why is there no owner check?] So that a change the owner queued cannot be stalled. → What does that assume? That the moment of the change has no economic effect. But for `setBeneficiaries`, the moment decides which table splits the balance that has not been sent out yet.

[Inversion: applyQueued]
1. A new-table payee calls `applyQueued(setBeneficiaries(T2))` and then `distribute(tokenX)` for each token in one transaction, so T2 splits the balance that built up under T1.
2. A beneficiary calls it from inside `distribute` during a push. `notLocked` stops this.
3. The action is `acceptOwnership` with `pendingOwner == this`. That only harms the owner, so I dropped it.

[Feynman: release/claim] These pay held amounts, by retry or by the account itself. They take the lock and cannot touch other accounts.

[Inversion: claim] (a) The `to` address re-enters during the ETH send: the lock is held. (b) A self-call of `claim` sees msg.sender == this, but this address never has a held amount, because a push to itself always works. (c) An ERC-777 hook on `to` hurts only the person who claims.

[Feynman: App] The owner stores the web page in chunks and serves them, then freezes them. `_requireChunk` accepts only code that starts with 0x00. Code that starts with STOP can never run, so it can never destroy itself, and an EIP-7702 designator (0xef01…) is refused.

[Inversion: App.lock] (1) A 7702 pointer: refused. (2) A metamorphic chunk: code that starts with 0x00 cannot run SELFDESTRUCT. (3) Version or chunks after lock: guarded. No seam found.

Agent 4 (execution-trace) returned 2 findings and 3 leads:
- **Finding:** in `distribute`, the ERC-20 transfer passes on all gas and copies all return data. A beneficiary of a hook token (ERC-777 style) can use that to make `distribute` fail for every caller.
- **Finding:** in `DistributionFactory.create`, the clone address does not commit to its settings. Agent 2 raised the same issue as a lead.

9 of 12 back. Waiting on agents 7, 11 and 12.

Agent 11 (trust-gap) returned 1 finding and 3 leads. The finding is that the clone address does not commit to its owner or table. That makes 3 agents on it (2 findings, 1 lead). Two agents still running: 7 and 12.

[Feynman: Distribution] Each clone holds money for a fixed list of payees. Anyone can tell it to split everything it holds that is not already set aside. A payee whose payment fails gets its share set aside in a per-token, per-payee bucket. "Set aside" is kept per token key, and `address(0)` stands for the chain's own coin. Fuzzy spot: the code treats `address(0)` and every ERC-20 address as separate pools of money. It never asks whether two keys can be the same money.

[Feynman: distribute] It reads the balance for the key, subtracts the amount set aside for that key, and pays each row. The ETH path caps each payee's gas. The ERC-20 path gives the token call all remaining gas and trusts that "the token bounds it". Fuzzy spot: the token is bounded, but the payee is not, if the token calls back into the payee.

[Feynman: release / claim] They move a bucket out. `release` retries the same push. `claim` lets the payee pick a destination.

[Feynman: propose / applyQueued / cancel / transferOwnership / acceptOwnership] This is a Compound-style timelock. The owner queues a call the contract makes to itself. Anyone can apply it after its eta, until eta plus `GRACE`. A handover or a renounce clears the queue.

[Feynman: DistributionFactory.create / predict] It places a PUSH0 clone with CREATE2. The top 20 bytes of the salt must equal the sender. It then calls `init`.

[Feynman: App] It serves chunks stored with SSTORE2, and `lock()` freezes them. `_requireChunk` accepts only code whose first byte is `0x00`.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:158 — why is `reserved[token]` the only subtraction?] Because the code believes one balance belongs to exactly one key. Why believe that? Because on Ethereum, native ETH and ERC-20 balances are separate ledgers. Does that hold on every chain this factory targets ("the same clone address on every chain")? No. On Celo, `CELO.balanceOf(x) == x.balance`, so the native coin has two keys and two `reserved` buckets.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:402-404 — why is the ERC-20 push uncapped?] Because "a hostile token's return data costs only the caller who named it." That covers the token's return data. It does not cover gas used by a recipient hook (ERC-777 `tokensReceived`), which the beneficiary controls, not the caller.

[Inversion: distribute] (1) On Celo, escrow native CELO for payee A, then call `distribute(CELO_ERC20)`. The balance check does not see `reserved[address(0)]`. (2) Use a beneficiary with an ERC-777 hook that burns gas, so the 1/64 left is too small for the remaining rows. (3) A rebasing token loses balance after an escrow, so `_balance - reserved` underflows and reverts.

[Inversion: applyQueued/cancel during the lock] A payee's receive calls `applyQueued`, and `notLocked` reverts. A payee's receive calls `cancel` or `acceptOwnership`, which change no table and move no money. A self-call action of `claim`, `propose` or `init` fails on its `msg.sender` check, or is harmless. The path holds.

[Inversion: App.lock] (1) A 7702 designator starts with `0xef`, so it is refused. (2) A codeless pointer is refused. (3) A contract that starts with `0x00` stops on byte 0, so it cannot run SELFDESTRUCT and its code is fixed. The path holds.

[Inversion: DistributionFactory.create] (1) Another sender reuses the salt: the prefix check refuses it. (2) Someone calls `init` on the implementation: `msg.sender` is not the factory, so it fails. (3) The two `mstore(0x24, …)` calls change the top bytes of the free memory pointer and then restore them, and nothing allocates memory in between. The path holds.

Net: B takes 25 of A's escrowed 50, and later depositors fund the rest.

The ERC-20 path gives the token call all remaining gas and trusts that "the token bounds it". Fuzzy spot: the token is bounded, but the payee is not, if the token calls back into the payee.

[Feynman: release / claim] They move a bucket out. `release` retries the same push. `claim` lets the payee pick a destination.

[Feynman: propose / applyQueued / cancel / transferOwnership / acceptOwnership] This is a Compound-style timelock. The owner queues a call the contract makes to itself. Anyone can apply it after its eta, until eta plus `GRACE`. A handover or a renounce clears the queue.

[Feynman: DistributionFactory.create / predict] It places a PUSH0 clone with CREATE2. The top 20 bytes of the salt must equal the sender. It then calls `init`.

[Feynman: App] It serves chunks stored with SSTORE2, and `lock()` freezes them. `_requireChunk` accepts only code whose first byte is `0x00`.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:158 — why is `reserved[token]` the only subtraction?] Because the code believes one balance belongs to exactly one key. Why believe that? Because on Ethereum, native ETH and ERC-20 balances are separate ledgers. Does that hold on every chain this factory targets ("the same clone address on every chain")? No. On Celo, `CELO.balanceOf(x) == x.balance`, so the native coin has two keys and two `reserved` buckets.

[Socratic: Distribution.sol:402-404 — why is the ERC-20 push uncapped?] Because "a hostile token's return data costs only the caller who named it." That covers the token's return data. It does not cover gas used by a recipient hook (ERC-777 `tokensReceived`), which the beneficiary controls, not the caller.

[Inversion: distribute] (1) On Celo, escrow native CELO for payee A, then call `distribute(CELO_ERC20)`. The balance check does not see `reserved[address(0)]`. (2) Use a beneficiary with an ERC-777 hook that burns gas, so the 1/64 left is too small for the remaining rows. (3) A rebasing token loses balance after an escrow, so `_balance - reserved` underflows and reverts.

[Inversion: applyQueued/cancel during the lock] A payee's receive calls `applyQueued`, and `notLocked` reverts. A payee's receive calls `cancel` or `acceptOwnership`, which change no table and move no money. A self-call action of `claim`, `propose` or `init` fails on its `msg.sender` check, or is harmless. The path holds.

[Inversion: App.lock] (1) A 7702 designator starts with `0xef`, so it is refused. (2) A codeless pointer is refused. (3) A contract that starts with `0x00` stops on byte 0, so it cannot run SELFDESTRUCT and its code is fixed. The path holds.

[Inversion: DistributionFactory.create] (1) Another sender reuses the salt: the prefix check refuses it. (2) Someone calls `init` on the implementation: `msg.sender` is not the factory, so it fails. (3) The two `mstore(0x24, …)` calls change the top bytes of the free memory pointer and then restore them, and nothing allocates memory in between. The path holds.
